title: Demand & Consumer Surplus

learningObjectives.text: Know and understand the following concepts: market demand curve, law of demand, change in quantity demanded, shift in demand, normal good, inferior good, substitute, complement, demand function, inverse demand function, consumer surplus
Know and understand how to construct and plot a demand curve
Know how to calculate the revenue maximizing price using calculus
Know how to calculate consumer surplus and describe what it means
Know and understand the four major categories or sources of product or service differentiation
learningObjectives.src: course-data.js Session 7 (taught in the 'Differentiation Advantage' LearnStrategy video — transcript not in materials)

keyTerms.def: Shows the total quantity of a good that all consumers in the market would purchase at each price, holding other factors constant.
Price and quantity demanded are inversely related: a price increase leads to a decrease in quantity demanded (and vice versa), all else equal.
keyTerms.src: S08 slides p.16 (applied); GENERAL ECON wording

keyTerms.def: A movement ALONG a demand curve caused by a change in the good's own price.
The whole curve moves (left = decrease, right = increase) because a non-price determinant changed: income, prices of related goods, advertising/consumer tastes, population, expectations.
keyTerms.src: GENERAL ECON (B&P Ch 2 topic); determinants listed in S05 slides p.41 and Math Review p.9

keyTerms.def: Demand increases when income rises; the coefficient on income in a demand function is positive.
keyTerms.src: CQ4 Q2 feedback (sign logic); Regression Exercise step 6 (Kimball)

keyTerms.def: Demand decreases when income rises; the coefficient on income is negative.
An increase in the price of good y raises demand for good x; the coefficient on Py is positive (CPE > 0).
keyTerms.src: CQ4 Q1 feedback; S08 slides p.27, p.29

keyTerms.def: An increase in the price of good y lowers demand for good x; the coefficient on Py is negative (CPE < 0), e.g., milk and cereal.
Quantity as a function of price (and other variables), e.g., Qx = 10,000 − 4Px + 5Py − 0.2I.
Price on the left, as a function of quantity: solve the demand function for P. E.g., Qx = 4,500 − 4Px → Px = 1,125 − 0.25Qx.
The area under the demand curve and above the price: the value consumers receive beyond what they pay. For linear demand, a triangle = ½ × quantity × (choke price − price).
keyTerms.src: CQ4 Q4 feedback; meaning = GENERAL ECON

keyTerms.def: The price where quantity demanded hits zero (the vertical intercept of demand).

workedExamples.answer: Quantity at each price = cumulative count of respondents willing to pay at least that price; scale sample to market with a market-to-sample ratio (e.g., ×300)

workedExamples.name: Demand curves are dynamic
workedExamples.answer: Demand shifted left (streaming substitutes) and became less price-sensitive among remaining customers; Kimball's fits: 2011 Q = 8,845 − 3,728P; 2014 Q = 7,019 − 2,426P
workedExamples.src: S07 slides p.32; S09 slides p.4; Differentiation Advantage Part 2

cases: A/B testing: Microsoft Bing 2012 ad-headline tweak → 12% revenue increase, ~$100M/year; Microsoft, Amazon, Facebook, Google each run >10,000 online experiments annually; Booking.com: 'our predictions of how customers behave are wrong nine times out of ten' (S07 slides pp.11-12, WSJ Mar 15, 2020)
Behavioral nudges: UK tax letter '9 out of 10 people in your town have paid'; opt-out organ donation (S07 slides p.13)
Same Job, Different Cost: Netflix MCPEH ≈ $0.10 vs. Redbox ≈ $0.52-0.65 (S07 slides p.5)
Scale economies work in reverse: Redbox ATC = 656.06R^−0.476, R² = 0.7519 (S07 slides p.6)
Look at the trend, not the snapshot: total expense as % of revenue — Netflix 220% (2001) → 106% at IPO (May 2002) → 93%; Blockbuster 94% → 95% (S07 slides p.7)
Redbox 2009-2015: kiosks, revenue per rental, rentals per kiosk (S07 slides pp.20-26)
traps: Own-price change → movement along the curve; anything else → shift
Inverse demand puts P on the left; don't confuse slope of Q-on-P (−b) with slope of P-on-Q (−1/b)
Substitute in the demand-shifter values BEFORE inverting
CS uses the choke price (where Q = 0), not the current price alone
